mcqs.question: Which of the following changes will most increase the magnetic field strength of an electromagnet?

options.A: Decrease the number of turns in the coil
options.B: Increase the current flowing through the coil
options.C: Replace the iron core with a non‑magnetic material
options.D: Increase the spacing between successive turns

mcqs.answer: Increase the current flowing through the coil
mcqs.explanation: The magnetic field strength (B) of an electromagnet is directly proportional to the product of the number of turns (N) and the current (I) (B ∝ N·I). Raising the current therefore increases the field strength. Decreasing turns, using a non‑magnetic core, or increasing spacing all reduce the field.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is a common practical application of an electromagnet?
mcqs.explanation: Door‑bells use a coil that becomes magnetised when current passes, attracting a metal striker to produce sound. The other devices do not rely on magnetic fields generated by current.

mcqs.question: A solenoid is best described as:

options.A: A tightly wound coil of wire that produces a uniform magnetic field inside when electric current passes through it
options.B: A permanent magnet shaped like a cylinder
options.C: A device that converts chemical energy directly into electrical energy
options.D: A type of battery that stores magnetic energy

mcqs.answer: A tightly wound coil of wire that produces a uniform magnetic field inside when electric current passes through it
mcqs.explanation: A solenoid consists of many turns of conducting wire. When current flows, the magnetic field lines inside become parallel and nearly uniform, similar to a bar magnet. It is not a permanent magnet or a power source.

mcqs.learning_point: Understand magnetic field of a solenoid
mcqs.question: What is the direction of the magnetic field inside a long solenoid when current flows clockwise as seen from one end?

options.A: From the north pole to the south pole, i.e., along the axis from that end toward the opposite end
options.B: Circular around each individual wire only
options.C: Uniform and parallel to the axis, pointing away from the observer at the end where the current appears clockwise
options.D: Randomly oriented with no definite direction

mcqs.answer: Uniform and parallel to the axis, pointing away from the observer at the end where the current appears clockwise
mcqs.explanation: Using the right‑hand rule, curl the fingers in the direction of the current (clockwise as seen). The thumb points toward the solenoid’s north pole, indicating the magnetic field direction inside the coil. Options B and D are incorrect descriptions, and A reverses the direction.

mcqs.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes an electromagnet from a permanent magnet?

options.A: An electromagnet requires electric current to produce a magnetic field, whereas a permanent magnet does not need any current.
options.B: An electromagnet is always stronger than any permanent magnet.
options.C: A permanent magnet can be turned off by disconnecting a power source.
options.D: Electromagnets are made only of iron, while permanent magnets are made of copper.

mcqs.answer: An electromagnet requires electric current to produce a magnetic field, whereas a permanent magnet does not need any current.
mcqs.explanation: The defining feature of an electromagnet is that its magnetic field exists only while current flows through its coil. Permanent magnets retain magnetisation without external power. Strength depends on design, not a universal rule, and material composition statements are false.

mcqs.question: To make an electromagnet stronger, which factor should be increased?

options.A: Number of turns of wire in the coil
options.B: Length of the wire used without adding turns

mcqs.answer: Number of turns of wire in the coil
mcqs.explanation: Magnetic field strength is proportional to the product of current (I) and number of turns (N). Increasing N directly enhances the field. Increasing length without adding turns raises resistance, reducing current. Higher resistance and a non‑magnetic core both weaken the field.

mcqs.question: Which of the following devices relies on an electromagnet to operate?
mcqs.explanation: MRI scanners use powerful electromagnets to create a uniform magnetic field for imaging. Light bulbs, solar cells, and thermos flasks do not employ electromagnets.

mcqs.question: A student wraps insulated copper wire tightly around a nail, connects the ends to a battery, and the nail attracts paper clips. Which description best fits this arrangement?

options.A: It is a simple electromagnet formed by a solenoid wound around a ferromagnetic core.
options.B: It is a permanent magnet that has been magnetised permanently.
options.C: It is a battery that stores electrical energy.
options.D: It is a resistor that limits current flow.

mcqs.answer: It is a simple electromagnet formed by a solenoid wound around a ferromagnetic core.
mcqs.explanation: The wire wound around the nail constitutes a solenoid; when current from the battery passes, the nail becomes magnetised (an electromagnet) and can attract ferromagnetic objects. It is not a permanent magnet, battery, or resistor.
